artboards.title: A - One method, one scope choice

annotations.text:
The model changed, not just the layout.

Every earlier design treated a SITE as the subject. That was wrong. The method that defeats a block belongs to the PROVIDER, not the site: it is the same DPI box inspecting every name, so a strategy that fools it for discord.com fools it for anything blocked the same way.

So the subject is "my provider's block and what defeats it", and the sites become a scope list plus the names used to prove it still works. Per-site scoping exists for exactly one reason - anti-cheat software reacts to a driver that watches every connection - not because strategies differ per site.

One consequence worth designing around: the names you add do two different jobs that were previously conflated. They are the targets a method is measured against, and they are what the kernel filter covers. In machine-wide mode the second job disappears and the first remains.

A - One method, one scope choice  (recommended)

The headline states what your provider does and what beats it. Below it, the only real decision: machine-wide or listed names, each with its honest cost. The list sits at the bottom, relabelled "checked against" - it proves the method rather than defining the product.

Shown on the TurkNet case, where the block is DNS-only. That is worth surfacing loudly: no driver is needed, so machine-wide costs nothing and is the right default there.

Tradeoff: it merges the two layers into one story. When only one of them is broken that is a simplification; when both are, you lose the ability to scope them separately.

B - A scope per layer

Shows the truth: there are two mechanisms, and each can be off, cover listed names, or cover the machine. Address lookups fix with a resolver change or hosts pins; the connection fixes with a driver.

Shown on the Vodafone case where BOTH layers are censored - the situation A has to simplify. Note the two scopes differ here on purpose: machine-wide DNS is free, machine-wide driver is not.

Tradeoff: two controls and a vocabulary to learn. It is the most honest and the least simple.

C - One switch

One toggle, one segmented scope control, the list folded to a single line, everything else behind Advanced.

The simplest thing that could work, and it fits the model: one method, one scope.

Tradeoff - the real one: it cannot say "the DNS half is fixed and the traffic half is not", which is exactly the half-fixed state this tool has already shipped a false success from. A single switch has to claim yes or no.
